draft.title: Tables of values from a rule
card: A rule links \(x\) and \(y\). To find \(y\), put a value of \(x\) into the rule and work it out.
Take the rule \(y = 2x + 1\). When \(x = 3\), \(y = 2 \times 3 + 1\), which is \(6 + 1 = 7\). Multiply first, then add.
Do this for each \(x\) value to fill a table. For \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3\), the \(y\) values are \(1, 3, 5, 7\).
Each pair is a point: \((0, 1)\), \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\), \((3, 7)\). Plotted, the points lie in a straight line.

4.alt: The points \((0, 1)\), \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\) and \((3, 7)\) from the rule \(y = 2x + 1\), lying on a straight line going up to the right.

draft.remember: Put each \(x\) into the rule, work out \(y\), and each pair is a point to plot.

a.q: Using the rule \(y = 3x - 2\), what is \(y\) when \(x = 4\)?
a.why: \(y = 3 \times 4 - 2 = 12 - 2 = 10\). The option 14 comes from adding 2 instead of taking it away.

b.q: Mia fills a table for the rule \(y = 2x + 1\). Which pair of values is correct for her table?
b.why: \(y = 2 \times 5 + 1 = 10 + 1 = 11\). The option 12 comes from adding 1 before multiplying: \((5 + 1) \times 2\).
